<reason>B provides the stronger comparative case: mandatory consideration of an outside forecast can constrain institutional optimism without transferring decision-making authority. A raises meaningful manipulation and thin-market risks, but does not establish why those risks outweigh qualified, transparent market input. B answers both pressure questions directly and distinguishes profitable forecasting from merely moving prices. A’s closing incorrectly treats oversight and decision-window concerns as unanswered, despite B’s preceding closing addressing both. B’s safeguards remain imperfect, but its case requires useful scrutiny, not guaranteed honesty or automatic policy changes.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B dismantles A’s claim that formal input must mean either compulsory deference or meaningless paperwork: that dilemma would also condemn advisory expert panels. Preannounced quality criteria and publicly reviewable explanations provide a middle position, with scrutiny occurring before commitment rather than only after settlement.</best_rebuttal>
